idiom_name: cookie-carried session id + own session table (Apache mod_session / mod_session_dbd shows the shape)
implementation_notes: C has no session framework, so the pattern is assembled from primitives: read the session id from the Cookie request header (or the server library's cookie API), mint it with a CSPRNG such as getrandom(2), keep the payload in a mutex-guarded hash table or a SQL table, and answer with a Set-Cookie header that carries only the id. Apache httpd's mod_session plus mod_session_dbd is the closest stock C realization - it stores the session value in a database row keyed either by an anonymous UUID cookie or by the authenticated userid, hides the payload from the browser, and lets several web servers share the same session database. Nothing replaces the classic structure here; writing it by hand is justified whenever an embedded HTTP server (CivetWeb, Mongoose) must offer sessions.
pitfalls: The session table is shared mutable state: without a mutex (or per-worker sharding) concurrent requests corrupt it, and a correct lock discipline is easy to lose when the table is touched from completion callbacks.
Session ids must come from a CSPRNG (getrandom(2) or /dev/urandom), never from rand(), time() or a counter; and every record must be freed on expiry or the table leaks.

Most C servers are multi-process or multi-worker by construction, so an in-process table loses sessions across workers; a shared store (mod_session_dbd's SQL tables, or an external cache) is the only way to keep the conversation.
